column10: [CSX LogoJACKSONVILLE, Fla., July 07, 2023 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- CSX (NASDAQ: CSX) announced the release of its 2022 Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) Report highlighting significant progress the company has made towards advancing its workforce and improving environmental stewardship, social responsibility and governance best practices over the past year.“2022 was a pivotal year for CSX,” said Joe Hinrichs, CSX president and chief executive officer. “Led by railroaders who are deservedly proud of their role in moving America’s freight, our employees began creating a ONE CSX culture in which we’re working together as a more unified team – one that operates more safely, efficiently and sustainably to serve our customers better and grow our business.”The report details CSX’s expanded use of cutting-edge fuel-saving locomotive technologies and its engagement of suppliers around GHG goals and expectations. Among its notable achievements, the company:Upgraded approximately 180 locomotives to distributed power, which moves more freight with less fuel;Engaged 50 suppliers – representing 75% of spend – in CDP’s Supply Chain program; andHelped customers avoid approximately 12.5 million tons of CO2 emissions.CSX also took concrete and historic actions to improve labor-management relations and quality of life for front-line employees. As part of these efforts, the report details the company’s advancement of its ONE CSX workplace culture rooted in valuing and developing its employees and built on teamwork across all levels, departments and locations. Notable accomplishments included:Becoming the first in the industry to provide paid sick leave benefits;Raising training pay for conductors by 40% – the highest increase for rail employees in more than 50 years; andIntroducing a revised non-disciplinary and non-punitive attendance policy for all craft employees.Hinrichs said, "At CSX, we are committed to delivering excellence. This means fostering stronger relationships with our employees, providing exceptional service to our customers, prioritizing environmental stewardship for the benefit of our communities, and adhering to the highest governance standards, all of which deliver strong shareholder value. We take great pride in our service product, and we remain dedicated to constant improvement as we move forward."Story continuesThe CSX report adheres to leading ESG disclosure frameworks including the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) 2021 Universal Standards, the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB) Rail Transportation standards and the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD).For more information on the company’s Environmental, Social and Governance efforts, review the 2022 CSX ESG Report and corresponding fact sheet, available online at csx.com/esg or the investor section of csx.com.About CSX CSX, based in Jacksonville, Florida, is a premier transportation company. It provides rail, intermodal and rail-to-truck transload services and solutions to customers across a broad array of markets, including energy, industrial, construction, agricultural, and consumer products. For nearly 200 years, CSX has played a critical role in the nation's economic expansion and industrial development. Its network connects every major metropolitan area in the eastern United States, where nearly two-thirds of the nation's population resides. It also links more than 240 short-line railroads and more than 70 ocean, river and lake ports with major population centers and farming towns alike.Contact:Matthew Korn, CFA, Investor Relations904-366-4515Bryan Tucker, Corporate Communications855-955-6397]

column4: AAR sues Ohio over 2-person train crew law
column10: [CSX operates in Ohio, where there is a new state law governing train crew sizes. (Photo: Jim Allen/FreightWaves)The Association of American Railroads (AAR) has filed a lawsuit against the state of Ohio, saying federal law preempts a new state law that dictates a minimum crew size for freight rail operations.Ohio’s law, signed by Gov. Mike DeWine on March 31, requires at least two individuals to be involved in moving a freight train in Ohio. The state may issue civil penalties for violations.A number of federal laws preempt Ohio’s law, argued AAR in a petition filed June 29 with the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio. These include the Regional Rail Reorganization Act of 1973 or 3R Act, which came out of freight rail service disruptions in the Northeast and Midwest; the ICC Termination Act, which grants the Surface Transportation Board authority to regulate certain matters; and the Federal Railroad Safety Act.The only Class I railroads that operate in the state are Canadian railway CN (NYSE: CNI), CSX (NASDAQ: CSX) and Norfolk Southern (NYSE: NSC). CSX and NS currently use single-person crews for certain yard operations, including remote control switching operations, AAR said.Ohio law is also more restrictive than a proposed regulation currently before the Federal Railroad Administration on train crew size because FRA’s rule would exempt particular types of trains or trains under specified conditions and has a special approval process for existing one-person crew operations, according to AAR. But Ohio’s law applies to every train or light engine used in connection with the movement of freight, with limited exceptions, AAR said.AAR also cited two studies from consulting firms Oliver Wyman and ICF International, which determined that available safety data and accident rates show no adverse safety impacts resulting from one-person crews versus two-person crews.AAR’s members will “suffer harm to their rights to collectively bargain over crew size. The carriers that operate in Ohio have the right to bargain for system-wide changes in crew size. The Crew Size Law will interfere with the railroads’ ability to expand their rights to operate with one-person crews in Ohio through collective bargaining,” attorneys for AAR said in the court filing.Story continuesCalifornia, Wisconsin, West Virginia, Arizona, Kansas, Minnesota, Washington, Nevada and Colorado also have state laws requiring freight train crews to have at least two people on board, according to the International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail, and Transportation Workers – Transportation Division (SMART-TD).States that have or have had legislation that calls for two-person crews include Illinois, New York and Pennsylvania, SMART-TD said.Subscribe to FreightWaves’ e-newsletters and get the latest insights on freight right in your inboxClick here for more FreightWaves articles by Joanna Marsh.Related links:Sick leave, crew consists still on the table between unions, railroadsTrain length and train crew sizes see state legislative actionUnion Pacific, SMART-TD agree to suspend train crew reconfigurationNS, SMART-TD to hold off on conductor redeployment talksTrain crew size bill advances in New Mexico LegislatureThe post AAR sues Ohio over 2-person train crew law appeared first on FreightWaves.]

column4: Investors Will Want CSX's (NASDAQ:CSX) Growth In ROCE To Persist
column10: [If we want to find a stock that could multiply over the long term, what are the underlying trends we should look for? Amongst other things, we'll want to see two things; firstly, a growing return on capital employed (ROCE) and secondly, an expansion in the company's amount of capital employed. This shows us that it's a compounding machine, able to continually reinvest its earnings back into the business and generate higher returns. So on that note, CSX (NASDAQ:CSX) looks quite promising in regards to its trends of return on capital.What Is Return On Capital Employed (ROCE)?For those who don't know, ROCE is a measure of a company's yearly pre-tax profit (its return), relative to the capital employed in the business. To calculate this metric for CSX, this is the formula:Return on Capital Employed = Earnings Before Interest and Tax (EBIT) ÷ (Total Assets - Current Liabilities)0.16 = US$6.1b ÷ (US$41b - US$2.3b) (Based on the trailing twelve months to March 2023).So, CSX has an ROCE of 16%.  In absolute terms, that's a pretty normal return, and it's somewhat close to the Transportation industry average of 14%. Basically the business is generating higher returns from the same amount of capital and that is proof that there are improvements in the company's efficiencies. It's worth looking deeper into this though because while it's great that the business is more efficient, it might also mean that going forward the areas to invest internally for the organic growth are lacking.Story continuesThe Bottom Line On CSX's ROCETo bring it all together, CSX has done well to increase the returns it's generating from its capital employed. column4: AAR sues Ohio over 2-person train crew law
column10: [CSX operates in Ohio, where there is a new state law governing train crew sizes. (Photo: Jim Allen/FreightWaves)The Association of American Railroads (AAR) has filed a lawsuit against the state of Ohio, saying federal law preempts a new state law that dictates a minimum crew size for freight rail operations.Ohio’s law, signed by Gov. Mike DeWine on March 31, requires at least two individuals to be involved in moving a freight train in Ohio. The state may issue civil penalties for violations.A number of federal laws preempt Ohio’s law, argued AAR in a petition filed June 29 with the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio. These include the Regional Rail Reorganization Act of 1973 or 3R Act, which came out of freight rail service disruptions in the Northeast and Midwest; the ICC Termination Act, which grants the Surface Transportation Board authority to regulate certain matters; and the Federal Railroad Safety Act.The only Class I railroads that operate in the state are Canadian railway CN (NYSE: CNI), CSX (NASDAQ: CSX) and Norfolk Southern (NYSE: NSC). CSX and NS currently use single-person crews for certain yard operations, including remote control switching operations, AAR said.Ohio law is also more restrictive than a proposed regulation currently before the Federal Railroad Administration on train crew size because FRA’s rule would exempt particular types of trains or trains under specified conditions and has a special approval process for existing one-person crew operations, according to AAR. But Ohio’s law applies to every train or light engine used in connection with the movement of freight, with limited exceptions, AAR said.AAR also cited two studies from consulting firms Oliver Wyman and ICF International, which determined that available safety data and accident rates show no adverse safety impacts resulting from one-person crews versus two-person crews.AAR’s members will “suffer harm to their rights to collectively bargain over crew size. The carriers that operate in Ohio have the right to bargain for system-wide changes in crew size. The Crew Size Law will interfere with the railroads’ ability to expand their rights to operate with one-person crews in Ohio through collective bargaining,” attorneys for AAR said in the court filing.Story continuesCalifornia, Wisconsin, West Virginia, Arizona, Kansas, Minnesota, Washington, Nevada and Colorado also have state laws requiring freight train crews to have at least two people on board, according to the International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail, and Transportation Workers – Transportation Division (SMART-TD).States that have or have had legislation that calls for two-person crews include Illinois, New York and Pennsylvania, SMART-TD said.Subscribe to FreightWaves’ e-newsletters and get the latest insights on freight right in your inboxClick here for more FreightWaves articles by Joanna Marsh.Related links:Sick leave, crew consists still on the table between unions, railroadsTrain length and train crew sizes see state legislative actionUnion Pacific, SMART-TD agree to suspend train crew reconfigurationNS, SMART-TD to hold off on conductor redeployment talksTrain crew size bill advances in New Mexico LegislatureThe post AAR sues Ohio over 2-person train crew law appeared first on FreightWaves.]

column4: Investors Will Want CSX's (NASDAQ:CSX) Growth In ROCE To Persist
column10: [If we want to find a stock that could multiply over the long term, what are the underlying trends we should look for? Amongst other things, we'll want to see two things; firstly, a growing return on capital employed (ROCE) and secondly, an expansion in the company's amount of capital employed. This shows us that it's a compounding machine, able to continually reinvest its earnings back into the business and generate higher returns. So on that note, CSX (NASDAQ:CSX) looks quite promising in regards to its trends of return on capital.What Is Return On Capital Employed (ROCE)?For those who don't know, ROCE is a measure of a company's yearly pre-tax profit (its return), relative to the capital employed in the business. To calculate this metric for CSX, this is the formula:Return on Capital Employed = Earnings Before Interest and Tax (EBIT) ÷ (Total Assets - Current Liabilities)0.16 = US$6.1b ÷ (US$41b - US$2.3b) (Based on the trailing twelve months to March 2023).So, CSX has an ROCE of 16%.  In absolute terms, that's a pretty normal return, and it's somewhat close to the Transportation industry average of 14%. Check out our latest analysis for CSX roceIn the above chart we have measured CSX's prior ROCE against its prior performance, but the future is arguably more important. If you'd like to see what analysts are forecasting going forward, you should check out our free report for CSX.How Are Returns Trending?CSX is showing promise given that its ROCE is trending up and to the right. More specifically, while the company has kept capital employed relatively flat over the last five years, the ROCE has climbed 39% in that same time. Basically the business is generating higher returns from the same amount of capital and that is proof that there are improvements in the company's efficiencies. It's worth looking deeper into this though because while it's great that the business is more efficient, it might also mean that going forward the areas to invest internally for the organic growth are lacking.Story continuesThe Bottom Line On CSX's ROCETo bring it all together, CSX has done well to increase the returns it's generating from its capital employed. And with a respectable 65% awarded to those who held the stock over the last five years, you could argue that these developments are starting to get the attention they deserve. column4: AAR sues Ohio over 2-person train crew law
column10: [CSX operates in Ohio, where there is a new state law governing train crew sizes. (Photo: Jim Allen/FreightWaves)The Association of American Railroads (AAR) has filed a lawsuit against the state of Ohio, saying federal law preempts a new state law that dictates a minimum crew size for freight rail operations.Ohio’s law, signed by Gov. Mike DeWine on March 31, requires at least two individuals to be involved in moving a freight train in Ohio. The state may issue civil penalties for violations.A number of federal laws preempt Ohio’s law, argued AAR in a petition filed June 29 with the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio. These include the Regional Rail Reorganization Act of 1973 or 3R Act, which came out of freight rail service disruptions in the Northeast and Midwest; the ICC Termination Act, which grants the Surface Transportation Board authority to regulate certain matters; and the Federal Railroad Safety Act.The only Class I railroads that operate in the state are Canadian railway CN (NYSE: CNI), CSX (NASDAQ: CSX) and Norfolk Southern (NYSE: NSC). CSX and NS currently use single-person crews for certain yard operations, including remote control switching operations, AAR said.Ohio law is also more restrictive than a proposed regulation currently before the Federal Railroad Administration on train crew size because FRA’s rule would exempt particular types of trains or trains under specified conditions and has a special approval process for existing one-person crew operations, according to AAR. But Ohio’s law applies to every train or light engine used in connection with the movement of freight, with limited exceptions, AAR said.AAR also cited two studies from consulting firms Oliver Wyman and ICF International, which determined that available safety data and accident rates show no adverse safety impacts resulting from one-person crews versus two-person crews.AAR’s members will “suffer harm to their rights to collectively bargain over crew size. The carriers that operate in Ohio have the right to bargain for system-wide changes in crew size. The Crew Size Law will interfere with the railroads’ ability to expand their rights to operate with one-person crews in Ohio through collective bargaining,” attorneys for AAR said in the court filing.Story continuesCalifornia, Wisconsin, West Virginia, Arizona, Kansas, Minnesota, Washington, Nevada and Colorado also have state laws requiring freight train crews to have at least two people on board, according to the International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail, and Transportation Workers – Transportation Division (SMART-TD).States that have or have had legislation that calls for two-person crews include Illinois, New York and Pennsylvania, SMART-TD said.Subscribe to FreightWaves’ e-newsletters and get the latest insights on freight right in your inboxClick here for more FreightWaves articles by Joanna Marsh.Related links:Sick leave, crew consists still on the table between unions, railroadsTrain length and train crew sizes see state legislative actionUnion Pacific, SMART-TD agree to suspend train crew reconfigurationNS, SMART-TD to hold off on conductor redeployment talksTrain crew size bill advances in New Mexico LegislatureThe post AAR sues Ohio over 2-person train crew law appeared first on FreightWaves.]

column10: [If we want to find a stock that could multiply over the long term, what are the underlying trends we should look for? Amongst other things, we'll want to see two things; firstly, a growing return on capital employed (ROCE) and secondly, an expansion in the company's amount of capital employed. This shows us that it's a compounding machine, able to continually reinvest its earnings back into the business and generate higher returns. So on that note, CSX (NASDAQ:CSX) looks quite promising in regards to its trends of return on capital.What Is Return On Capital Employed (ROCE)?For those who don't know, ROCE is a measure of a company's yearly pre-tax profit (its return), relative to the capital employed in the business. To calculate this metric for CSX, this is the formula:Return on Capital Employed = Earnings Before Interest and Tax (EBIT) ÷ (Total Assets - Current Liabilities)0.16 = US$6.1b ÷ (US$41b - US$2.3b) (Based on the trailing twelve months to March 2023).So, CSX has an ROCE of 16%.  In absolute terms, that's a pretty normal return, and it's somewhat close to the Transportation industry average of 14%. column4: AAR sues Ohio over 2-person train crew law
column10: [CSX operates in Ohio, where there is a new state law governing train crew sizes. (Photo: Jim Allen/FreightWaves)The Association of American Railroads (AAR) has filed a lawsuit against the state of Ohio, saying federal law preempts a new state law that dictates a minimum crew size for freight rail operations.Ohio’s law, signed by Gov. Mike DeWine on March 31, requires at least two individuals to be involved in moving a freight train in Ohio. The state may issue civil penalties for violations.A number of federal laws preempt Ohio’s law, argued AAR in a petition filed June 29 with the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio. These include the Regional Rail Reorganization Act of 1973 or 3R Act, which came out of freight rail service disruptions in the Northeast and Midwest; the ICC Termination Act, which grants the Surface Transportation Board authority to regulate certain matters; and the Federal Railroad Safety Act.The only Class I railroads that operate in the state are Canadian railway CN (NYSE: CNI), CSX (NASDAQ: CSX) and Norfolk Southern (NYSE: NSC). CSX and NS currently use single-person crews for certain yard operations, including remote control switching operations, AAR said.Ohio law is also more restrictive than a proposed regulation currently before the Federal Railroad Administration on train crew size because FRA’s rule would exempt particular types of trains or trains under specified conditions and has a special approval process for existing one-person crew operations, according to AAR. But Ohio’s law applies to every train or light engine used in connection with the movement of freight, with limited exceptions, AAR said.AAR also cited two studies from consulting firms Oliver Wyman and ICF International, which determined that available safety data and accident rates show no adverse safety impacts resulting from one-person crews versus two-person crews.AAR’s members will “suffer harm to their rights to collectively bargain over crew size. The carriers that operate in Ohio have the right to bargain for system-wide changes in crew size. The Crew Size Law will interfere with the railroads’ ability to expand their rights to operate with one-person crews in Ohio through collective bargaining,” attorneys for AAR said in the court filing.Story continuesCalifornia, Wisconsin, West Virginia, Arizona, Kansas, Minnesota, Washington, Nevada and Colorado also have state laws requiring freight train crews to have at least two people on board, according to the International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail, and Transportation Workers – Transportation Division (SMART-TD).States that have or have had legislation that calls for two-person crews include Illinois, New York and Pennsylvania, SMART-TD said.Subscribe to FreightWaves’ e-newsletters and get the latest insights on freight right in your inboxClick here for more FreightWaves articles by Joanna Marsh.Related links:Sick leave, crew consists still on the table between unions, railroadsTrain length and train crew sizes see state legislative actionUnion Pacific, SMART-TD agree to suspend train crew reconfigurationNS, SMART-TD to hold off on conductor redeployment talksTrain crew size bill advances in New Mexico LegislatureThe post AAR sues Ohio over 2-person train crew law appeared first on FreightWaves.]

column4: Investors Will Want CSX's (NASDAQ:CSX) Growth In ROCE To Persist
column10: [If we want to find a stock that could multiply over the long term, what are the underlying trends we should look for? Amongst other things, we'll want to see two things; firstly, a growing return on capital employed (ROCE) and secondly, an expansion in the company's amount of capital employed. This shows us that it's a compounding machine, able to continually reinvest its earnings back into the business and generate higher returns. So on that note, CSX (NASDAQ:CSX) looks quite promising in regards to its trends of return on capital.What Is Return On Capital Employed (ROCE)?For those who don't know, ROCE is a measure of a company's yearly pre-tax profit (its return), relative to the capital employed in the business. To calculate this metric for CSX, this is the formula:Return on Capital Employed = Earnings Before Interest and Tax (EBIT) ÷ (Total Assets - Current Liabilities)0.16 = US$6.1b ÷ (US$41b - US$2.3b) (Based on the trailing twelve months to March 2023).So, CSX has an ROCE of 16%.  In absolute terms, that's a pretty normal return, and it's somewhat close to the Transportation industry average of 14%. Check out our latest analysis for CSX roceIn the above chart we have measured CSX's prior ROCE against its prior performance, but the future is arguably more important. If you'd like to see what analysts are forecasting going forward, you should check out our free report for CSX.How Are Returns Trending?CSX is showing promise given that its ROCE is trending up and to the right. More specifically, while the company has kept capital employed relatively flat over the last five years, the ROCE has climbed 39% in that same time. Basically the business is generating higher returns from the same amount of capital and that is proof that there are improvements in the company's efficiencies. It's worth looking deeper into this though because while it's great that the business is more efficient, it might also mean that going forward the areas to invest internally for the organic growth are lacking.Story continuesThe Bottom Line On CSX's ROCETo bring it all together, CSX has done well to increase the returns it's generating from its capital employed. And with a respectable 65% awarded to those who held the stock over the last five years, you could argue that these developments are starting to get the attention they deserve. Mike DeWine on March 31, requires at least two individuals to be involved in moving a freight train in Ohio. The state may issue civil penalties for violations.A number of federal laws preempt Ohio’s law, argued AAR in a petition filed June 29 with the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio. These include the Regional Rail Reorganization Act of 1973 or 3R Act, which came out of freight rail service disruptions in the Northeast and Midwest; the ICC Termination Act, which grants the Surface Transportation Board authority to regulate certain matters; and the Federal Railroad Safety Act.The only Class I railroads that operate in the state are Canadian railway CN (NYSE: CNI), CSX (NASDAQ: CSX) and Norfolk Southern (NYSE: NSC). CSX and NS currently use single-person crews for certain yard operations, including remote control switching operations, AAR said.Ohio law is also more restrictive than a proposed regulation currently before the Federal Railroad Administration on train crew size because FRA’s rule would exempt particular types of trains or trains under specified conditions and has a special approval process for existing one-person crew operations, according to AAR. But Ohio’s law applies to every train or light engine used in connection with the movement of freight, with limited exceptions, AAR said.AAR also cited two studies from consulting firms Oliver Wyman and ICF International, which determined that available safety data and accident rates show no adverse safety impacts resulting from one-person crews versus two-person crews.AAR’s members will “suffer harm to their rights to collectively bargain over crew size. The carriers that operate in Ohio have the right to bargain for system-wide changes in crew size. The Crew Size Law will interfere with the railroads’ ability to expand their rights to operate with one-person crews in Ohio through collective bargaining,” attorneys for AAR said in the court filing.Story continuesCalifornia, Wisconsin, West Virginia, Arizona, Kansas, Minnesota, Washington, Nevada and Colorado also have state laws requiring freight train crews to have at least two people on board, according to the International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail, and Transportation Workers – Transportation Division (SMART-TD).States that have or have had legislation that calls for two-person crews include Illinois, New York and Pennsylvania, SMART-TD said.Subscribe to FreightWaves’ e-newsletters and get the latest insights on freight right in your inboxClick here for more FreightWaves articles by Joanna Marsh.Related links:Sick leave, crew consists still on the table between unions, railroadsTrain length and train crew sizes see state legislative actionUnion Pacific, SMART-TD agree to suspend train crew reconfigurationNS, SMART-TD to hold off on conductor redeployment talksTrain crew size bill advances in New Mexico LegislatureThe post AAR sues Ohio over 2-person train crew law appeared first on FreightWaves.]

column10: [If we want to find a stock that could multiply over the long term, what are the underlying trends we should look for? Amongst other things, we'll want to see two things; firstly, a growing return on capital employed (ROCE) and secondly, an expansion in the company's amount of capital employed. This shows us that it's a compounding machine, able to continually reinvest its earnings back into the business and generate higher returns. So on that note, CSX (NASDAQ:CSX) looks quite promising in regards to its trends of return on capital.What Is Return On Capital Employed (ROCE)?For those who don't know, ROCE is a measure of a company's yearly pre-tax profit (its return), relative to the capital employed in the business. To calculate this metric for CSX, this is the formula:Return on Capital Employed = Earnings Before Interest and Tax (EBIT) ÷ (Total Assets - Current Liabilities)0.16 = US$6.1b ÷ (US$41b - US$2.3b) (Based on the trailing twelve months to March 2023).So, CSX has an ROCE of 16%.  In absolute terms, that's a pretty normal return, and it's somewhat close to the Transportation industry average of 14%. According to IMARC Group's projections, the market is anticipated to reach $503.3 billion by 2028, indicating a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 4.11% during the forecast period from 2023 to 2028. Since global transportation demand is increasing rapidly, the International Energy Agency predicts that passenger and freight activity will double the current levels by 2050. While this is a sign of economic prosperity, it goes hand in hand with higher emissions and atmospheric damage. High speed railways are a perfect solution for a swiftly urbanizing world, as rail is considered one of the most energy efficient means of transport. Currently, about 75% of passengers use electric trains, compared to about 60% of the passengers boarding these energy efficient trains in 2000. As a result of this heavy reliance on electricity, the rail sector is the most diverse mode of transport in terms of energy sources. Europe, Japan, and Russia have the highest number of electric trains, while North and South America are largely reliant on diesel. Over the past two decades, there has been a consistent increase in freight rail activity. Currently, the movement of freight by rail is primarily concentrated in China and the United States, with each country accounting for about one-quarter of global rail freight activity. Additionally, Russia holds a prominent share, making up one-fifth of the global freight movement. The transportation of minerals, coal, and agricultural products constitutes the majority of freight rail activity worldwide.Don't Miss: Top 15 Railroad Companies In The WorldThe trade trends from CNBC Supply Chain Heat Map data have consistently demonstrated a decline in inbound freight over the last few months. This reduction in freight has had a negative impact on the earnings of both trucking and rail industries, as their revenue depends on the transportation of goods. According to United Parcel Service, Inc. (NYSE:UPS) CEO Carol Tome, a downturn in US retail sales and persistently weak demand in Asia contributed to lower-than-expected freight volume for the company. column4: Buy Vail Resorts & CSX, steer clear of CVS & FirstEnergy: Portfolio manager
column10: [Buy Vail Resorts to take advantage of consumer spending, but maybe wait hold off on CVS because of regulatory pressure on drug prices. Zacks Investment Management Client Portfolio Manager Brian Mulberry shares some of his top stock trades with Yahoo Finance Live.Video TranscriptAKIKO FUJITA: Well, the CPI data may have the markets moving today. But it's time to take a longer term look at the potential hotspots for investing in the second half of 2023. To give us his take on what stocks we should be buying right now and the ones to avoid, let's bring in Brian Mulberry, Client Portfolio Manager at Zacks Investment Management.We're going to start with your picks, what you like right now. Vail Resort, specifically, you're looking at the travel space right now. That stock not at the highs-- you know, still below the high of the year. But we have seen consumers, despite some headwinds and concerns about higher prices, shelling out on travel.BRIAN MULBERRY: Yeah, absolutely. It's a way to access the consumer in a slightly different way, where we're seeing the revenge travel trade is still occurring. What we're noticing about Vail in particular is that season pass sales are up about 6%. And they're having a really good recapture rate when it comes to renewing pass holders from last year. And on top of that, they've actually been able to increase prices. So actual sales in dollars are up 11% on that 6% higher season pass sale.So we're looking at a way to take advantage of the consumer spending that has been really durable over the last year. And it's one of the reasons we like Vail. Vail has also done a great job of providing a different menu of passes available and also different destinations. Now, international, we're seeing very strong demand for their resorts in Australia. And there's been some great cross-selling opportunities for consumers internationally to access the US mountains and markets, and then obviously, for US consumers to travel abroad.Story continuesAnd so we're definitely still seeing consumers spend money at a very high rate. And it's one of those ways that we can access this type of a stock at a good price that's still set to continue to grow.SEANA SMITH: But Brian, how should investors be looking at a name like this given the fact that we are still at a risk of recession. There is some signs that the consumer is cracking just a little bit, pulling back on some of their spending. Is a name like Vail, is that going to be able to withstand some of that volatility?BRIAN MULBERRY: We think it is, because there's definitely a big dividing line in the consumer right now. And it's simply this, if you owned your home during the pandemic, you had a once-in-a-generation opportunity to refinance your biggest debt, which is usually your mortgage, on your biggest asset, your home, that appreciated probably 30% to 40% in value. You're able to pay off your cars, your student loans, all these other debts and credit cards. And you now have a much cleaner personal balance sheet.Your personal net income is probably in much better shape than it ever was before. And that lends a little bit more consistency to this consumer spending picture that we're seeing. Unfortunately, if you didn't own your home, those are definitely the consumers that are feeling the pinch of high inflation as well as high interest rates at this point in time.And so we're definitely keeping a close eye on it. We're aware of it. But there is a way to still bet on the consumer. And we think this is one of the ways to do that.AKIKO FUJITA: Another stock you're really hot on, CSX. This is in the rail space. What do you like there?BRIAN MULBERRY: What we're seeing is just a really consistent level of volume, in terms of the rail traffic that they have. They've actually been able to grow by almost 40% in terms of their coal transportation. A lot of that coal is going to produce electricity in other places. And so they've been able to keep up with a really high level of demand. And the execution in the transportation space is one of those things that leads to better margins overall.So again, not a huge valuation. It's one of those ways to invest in something that doesn't have a gigantic PE forward multiple but also has really good, durable earnings. They're also rewarding shareholders by raising their dividend. They actually increase their dividend by 10% earlier this year. And so it's a way to be a little bit more defensive in your allocation.But we also believe that energy overall might be a better place in the second half of the year. And this is just a different way to access those types of returns. Looking at what we've seen in terms of the price of coal and now demand for it coming up, it's going to be a better back half of the year for these types of names in our opinion.SEANA SMITH: Brian, one of the names that you're advising investors to stay away from is CVS. We know the stock has been under pressure now for some time, off pretty significantly since the start of the year. What do you see as pressuring the company here going forward?BRIAN MULBERRY: Well, there's a couple of different reasons that we see, I think, a material decline in both profitability and overall earnings. And obviously, it's one being that they're not getting reimbursed for COVID testing and COVID vaccines at nearly the rate that they were a year or two years ago.But also, in addition to that, you know, there's a lot of regulatory pressure on prices at pharmacies for drugs. And that's good for consumers, but it's net bad for the balance sheet for somebody like CVS when we're seeing more generic drugs available but less reimbursement coming from distributing those generic drugs. It's kind of a double whammy on a company like CVS, where they're not getting the reimbursement from COVID protocols. And now, there's pressure on prices at the pharmacy, which is normally, you know, their top breadwinner, if you will, in terms of generating that revenue.So we think it's going to be a bit of a tough slog for CVS for the next couple of quarters until they can kind of get things figured out where their margins might be headed.AKIKO FUJITA: And finally, Brian, you were talking about some opportunities in the energy spaces. Next name-- next name not necessarily one that you would encourage investors to stay on top of. What are the concerns you have with FirstEnergy?BRIAN MULBERRY: FirstEnergy kind of has an aging grid, if you will. This is a power utility. And while there is a lot of demand for electricity, the way that it's been generated has not been profitable for them. And unfortunately, it's a publicly traded utility that has price caps, if you will. They have to get permission in order to raise their rates to be more profitable in most of the markets that they serve.They've been having a difficult time accessing equipment, maintaining equipment. And like I said, their aging grid is really just been a drag on their overall profitability. So this is one of those energy type names that we would avoid, because it just seems like their execution is a little bit behind the curve. And this is one of those things where certainly the supply chain has affected their ability to get the parts that they need to upgrade their grid and their distribution facilities for sure.But it's definitely weighing on their overall earnings and profitability picture. So this is a name that we would be cautious of in the next couple of quarters.SEANA SMITH: All right. Brian Mulberry of Zacks Investment Management, thanks.]

column4: AAR sues Ohio over 2-person train crew law
column10: [CSX operates in Ohio, where there is a new state law governing train crew sizes. (Photo: Jim Allen/FreightWaves)The Association of American Railroads (AAR) has filed a lawsuit against the state of Ohio, saying federal law preempts a new state law that dictates a minimum crew size for freight rail operations.Ohio’s law, signed by Gov. Mike DeWine on March 31, requires at least two individuals to be involved in moving a freight train in Ohio. The state may issue civil penalties for violations.A number of federal laws preempt Ohio’s law, argued AAR in a petition filed June 29 with the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio. These include the Regional Rail Reorganization Act of 1973 or 3R Act, which came out of freight rail service disruptions in the Northeast and Midwest; the ICC Termination Act, which grants the Surface Transportation Board authority to regulate certain matters; and the Federal Railroad Safety Act.The only Class I railroads that operate in the state are Canadian railway CN (NYSE: CNI), CSX (NASDAQ: CSX) and Norfolk Southern (NYSE: NSC). CSX and NS currently use single-person crews for certain yard operations, including remote control switching operations, AAR said.Ohio law is also more restrictive than a proposed regulation currently before the Federal Railroad Administration on train crew size because FRA’s rule would exempt particular types of trains or trains under specified conditions and has a special approval process for existing one-person crew operations, according to AAR. But Ohio’s law applies to every train or light engine used in connection with the movement of freight, with limited exceptions, AAR said.AAR also cited two studies from consulting firms Oliver Wyman and ICF International, which determined that available safety data and accident rates show no adverse safety impacts resulting from one-person crews versus two-person crews.AAR’s members will “suffer harm to their rights to collectively bargain over crew size. The carriers that operate in Ohio have the right to bargain for system-wide changes in crew size. The Crew Size Law will interfere with the railroads’ ability to expand their rights to operate with one-person crews in Ohio through collective bargaining,” attorneys for AAR said in the court filing.Story continuesCalifornia, Wisconsin, West Virginia, Arizona, Kansas, Minnesota, Washington, Nevada and Colorado also have state laws requiring freight train crews to have at least two people on board, according to the International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail, and Transportation Workers – Transportation Division (SMART-TD).States that have or have had legislation that calls for two-person crews include Illinois, New York and Pennsylvania, SMART-TD said.Subscribe to FreightWaves’ e-newsletters and get the latest insights on freight right in your inboxClick here for more FreightWaves articles by Joanna Marsh.Related links:Sick leave, crew consists still on the table between unions, railroadsTrain length and train crew sizes see state legislative actionUnion Pacific, SMART-TD agree to suspend train crew reconfigurationNS, SMART-TD to hold off on conductor redeployment talksTrain crew size bill advances in New Mexico LegislatureThe post AAR sues Ohio over 2-person train crew law appeared first on FreightWaves.]

column4: Investors Will Want CSX's (NASDAQ:CSX) Growth In ROCE To Persist
column10: [If we want to find a stock that could multiply over the long term, what are the underlying trends we should look for? Amongst other things, we'll want to see two things; firstly, a growing return on capital employed (ROCE) and secondly, an expansion in the company's amount of capital employed. This shows us that it's a compounding machine, able to continually reinvest its earnings back into the business and generate higher returns. So on that note, CSX (NASDAQ:CSX) looks quite promising in regards to its trends of return on capital.What Is Return On Capital Employed (ROCE)?For those who don't know, ROCE is a measure of a company's yearly pre-tax profit (its return), relative to the capital employed in the business. To calculate this metric for CSX, this is the formula:Return on Capital Employed = Earnings Before Interest and Tax (EBIT) ÷ (Total Assets - Current Liabilities)0.16 = US$6.1b ÷ (US$41b - US$2.3b) (Based on the trailing twelve months to March 2023).So, CSX has an ROCE of 16%.  In absolute terms, that's a pretty normal return, and it's somewhat close to the Transportation industry average of 14%. Check out our latest analysis for CSX roceIn the above chart we have measured CSX's prior ROCE against its prior performance, but the future is arguably more important. If you'd like to see what analysts are forecasting going forward, you should check out our free report for CSX.How Are Returns Trending?CSX is showing promise given that its ROCE is trending up and to the right. More specifically, while the company has kept capital employed relatively flat over the last five years, the ROCE has climbed 39% in that same time. Basically the business is generating higher returns from the same amount of capital and that is proof that there are improvements in the company's efficiencies. It's worth looking deeper into this though because while it's great that the business is more efficient, it might also mean that going forward the areas to invest internally for the organic growth are lacking.Story continuesThe Bottom Line On CSX's ROCETo bring it all together, CSX has done well to increase the returns it's generating from its capital employed. And with a respectable 65% awarded to those who held the stock over the last five years, you could argue that these developments are starting to get the attention they deserve. column4: Do CSX's (NASDAQ:CSX) Earnings Warrant Your Attention?
column10: [The excitement of investing in a company that can reverse its fortunes is a big draw for some speculators, so even companies that have no revenue, no profit, and a record of falling short, can manage to find investors. Unfortunately, these high risk investments often have little probability of ever paying off, and many investors pay a price to learn their lesson. While a well funded company may sustain losses for years, it will need to generate a profit eventually, or else investors will move on and the company will wither away.In contrast to all that, many investors prefer to focus on companies like CSX (NASDAQ:CSX), which has not only revenues, but also profits. Even if this company is fairly valued by the market, investors would agree that generating consistent profits will continue to provide CSX with the means to add long-term value to shareholders. See our latest analysis for CSX How Quickly Is CSX Increasing Earnings Per Share?If you believe that markets are even vaguely efficient, then over the long term you'd expect a company's share price to follow its earnings per share (EPS) outcomes. Therefore, there are plenty of investors who like to buy shares in companies that are growing EPS. CSX managed to grow EPS by 15% per year, over three years. That growth rate is fairly good, assuming the company can keep it up.Careful consideration of revenue growth and earnings before interest and taxation (EBIT) margins can help inform a view on the sustainability of the recent profit growth. While we note CSX achieved similar EBIT margins to last year, revenue grew by a solid 15% to US$15b. That's a real positive.In the chart below, you can see how the company has grown earnings and revenue, over time. This comes in at 0.3% of shares in the company, which is a fair amount of a business of this size. column4: Buy Vail Resorts & CSX, steer clear of CVS & FirstEnergy: Portfolio manager
column10: [Buy Vail Resorts to take advantage of consumer spending, but maybe wait hold off on CVS because of regulatory pressure on drug prices. Zacks Investment Management Client Portfolio Manager Brian Mulberry shares some of his top stock trades with Yahoo Finance Live.Video TranscriptAKIKO FUJITA: Well, the CPI data may have the markets moving today. But it's time to take a longer term look at the potential hotspots for investing in the second half of 2023. To give us his take on what stocks we should be buying right now and the ones to avoid, let's bring in Brian Mulberry, Client Portfolio Manager at Zacks Investment Management.We're going to start with your picks, what you like right now. Vail Resort, specifically, you're looking at the travel space right now. That stock not at the highs-- you know, still below the high of the year. But we have seen consumers, despite some headwinds and concerns about higher prices, shelling out on travel.BRIAN MULBERRY: Yeah, absolutely. It's a way to access the consumer in a slightly different way, where we're seeing the revenge travel trade is still occurring. What we're noticing about Vail in particular is that season pass sales are up about 6%. And they're having a really good recapture rate when it comes to renewing pass holders from last year. And on top of that, they've actually been able to increase prices. So actual sales in dollars are up 11% on that 6% higher season pass sale.So we're looking at a way to take advantage of the consumer spending that has been really durable over the last year. And it's one of the reasons we like Vail. Vail has also done a great job of providing a different menu of passes available and also different destinations. Now, international, we're seeing very strong demand for their resorts in Australia. And there's been some great cross-selling opportunities for consumers internationally to access the US mountains and markets, and then obviously, for US consumers to travel abroad.Story continuesAnd so we're definitely still seeing consumers spend money at a very high rate. And it's one of those ways that we can access this type of a stock at a good price that's still set to continue to grow.SEANA SMITH: But Brian, how should investors be looking at a name like this given the fact that we are still at a risk of recession. There is some signs that the consumer is cracking just a little bit, pulling back on some of their spending. Is a name like Vail, is that going to be able to withstand some of that volatility?BRIAN MULBERRY: We think it is, because there's definitely a big dividing line in the consumer right now. And it's simply this, if you owned your home during the pandemic, you had a once-in-a-generation opportunity to refinance your biggest debt, which is usually your mortgage, on your biggest asset, your home, that appreciated probably 30% to 40% in value. You're able to pay off your cars, your student loans, all these other debts and credit cards. And you now have a much cleaner personal balance sheet.Your personal net income is probably in much better shape than it ever was before. And that lends a little bit more consistency to this consumer spending picture that we're seeing. Unfortunately, if you didn't own your home, those are definitely the consumers that are feeling the pinch of high inflation as well as high interest rates at this point in time.And so we're definitely keeping a close eye on it. We're aware of it. But there is a way to still bet on the consumer. And we think this is one of the ways to do that.AKIKO FUJITA: Another stock you're really hot on, CSX. This is in the rail space. What do you like there?BRIAN MULBERRY: What we're seeing is just a really consistent level of volume, in terms of the rail traffic that they have. They've actually been able to grow by almost 40% in terms of their coal transportation. A lot of that coal is going to produce electricity in other places. And so they've been able to keep up with a really high level of demand. And the execution in the transportation space is one of those things that leads to better margins overall.So again, not a huge valuation. It's one of those ways to invest in something that doesn't have a gigantic PE forward multiple but also has really good, durable earnings. They're also rewarding shareholders by raising their dividend. They actually increase their dividend by 10% earlier this year. And so it's a way to be a little bit more defensive in your allocation.But we also believe that energy overall might be a better place in the second half of the year. And this is just a different way to access those types of returns. Looking at what we've seen in terms of the price of coal and now demand for it coming up, it's going to be a better back half of the year for these types of names in our opinion.SEANA SMITH: Brian, one of the names that you're advising investors to stay away from is CVS. We know the stock has been under pressure now for some time, off pretty significantly since the start of the year. What do you see as pressuring the company here going forward?BRIAN MULBERRY: Well, there's a couple of different reasons that we see, I think, a material decline in both profitability and overall earnings. And obviously, it's one being that they're not getting reimbursed for COVID testing and COVID vaccines at nearly the rate that they were a year or two years ago.But also, in addition to that, you know, there's a lot of regulatory pressure on prices at pharmacies for drugs. And that's good for consumers, but it's net bad for the balance sheet for somebody like CVS when we're seeing more generic drugs available but less reimbursement coming from distributing those generic drugs. It's kind of a double whammy on a company like CVS, where they're not getting the reimbursement from COVID protocols. What are the concerns you have with FirstEnergy?BRIAN MULBERRY: FirstEnergy kind of has an aging grid, if you will. This is a power utility. And unfortunately, it's a publicly traded utility that has price caps, if you will. column4: AAR sues Ohio over 2-person train crew law
column10: [CSX operates in Ohio, where there is a new state law governing train crew sizes. (Photo: Jim Allen/FreightWaves)The Association of American Railroads (AAR) has filed a lawsuit against the state of Ohio, saying federal law preempts a new state law that dictates a minimum crew size for freight rail operations.Ohio’s law, signed by Gov. Mike DeWine on March 31, requires at least two individuals to be involved in moving a freight train in Ohio. The state may issue civil penalties for violations.A number of federal laws preempt Ohio’s law, argued AAR in a petition filed June 29 with the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio. These include the Regional Rail Reorganization Act of 1973 or 3R Act, which came out of freight rail service disruptions in the Northeast and Midwest; the ICC Termination Act, which grants the Surface Transportation Board authority to regulate certain matters; and the Federal Railroad Safety Act.The only Class I railroads that operate in the state are Canadian railway CN (NYSE: CNI), CSX (NASDAQ: CSX) and Norfolk Southern (NYSE: NSC). CSX and NS currently use single-person crews for certain yard operations, including remote control switching operations, AAR said.Ohio law is also more restrictive than a proposed regulation currently before the Federal Railroad Administration on train crew size because FRA’s rule would exempt particular types of trains or trains under specified conditions and has a special approval process for existing one-person crew operations, according to AAR. But Ohio’s law applies to every train or light engine used in connection with the movement of freight, with limited exceptions, AAR said.AAR also cited two studies from consulting firms Oliver Wyman and ICF International, which determined that available safety data and accident rates show no adverse safety impacts resulting from one-person crews versus two-person crews.AAR’s members will “suffer harm to their rights to collectively bargain over crew size. The carriers that operate in Ohio have the right to bargain for system-wide changes in crew size. The Crew Size Law will interfere with the railroads’ ability to expand their rights to operate with one-person crews in Ohio through collective bargaining,” attorneys for AAR said in the court filing.Story continuesCalifornia, Wisconsin, West Virginia, Arizona, Kansas, Minnesota, Washington, Nevada and Colorado also have state laws requiring freight train crews to have at least two people on board, according to the International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail, and Transportation Workers – Transportation Division (SMART-TD).States that have or have had legislation that calls for two-person crews include Illinois, New York and Pennsylvania, SMART-TD said.Subscribe to FreightWaves’ e-newsletters and get the latest insights on freight right in your inboxClick here for more FreightWaves articles by Joanna Marsh.Related links:Sick leave, crew consists still on the table between unions, railroadsTrain length and train crew sizes see state legislative actionUnion Pacific, SMART-TD agree to suspend train crew reconfigurationNS, SMART-TD to hold off on conductor redeployment talksTrain crew size bill advances in New Mexico LegislatureThe post AAR sues Ohio over 2-person train crew law appeared first on FreightWaves.]

column4: Do CSX's (NASDAQ:CSX) Earnings Warrant Your Attention?
column10: [The excitement of investing in a company that can reverse its fortunes is a big draw for some speculators, so even companies that have no revenue, no profit, and a record of falling short, can manage to find investors. Unfortunately, these high risk investments often have little probability of ever paying off, and many investors pay a price to learn their lesson. While a well funded company may sustain losses for years, it will need to generate a profit eventually, or else investors will move on and the company will wither away.In contrast to all that, many investors prefer to focus on companies like CSX (NASDAQ:CSX), which has not only revenues, but also profits. Even if this company is fairly valued by the market, investors would agree that generating consistent profits will continue to provide CSX with the means to add long-term value to shareholders. See our latest analysis for CSX How Quickly Is CSX Increasing Earnings Per Share?If you believe that markets are even vaguely efficient, then over the long term you'd expect a company's share price to follow its earnings per share (EPS) outcomes. Therefore, there are plenty of investors who like to buy shares in companies that are growing EPS. CSX managed to grow EPS by 15% per year, over three years. That growth rate is fairly good, assuming the company can keep it up.Careful consideration of revenue growth and earnings before interest and taxation (EBIT) margins can help inform a view on the sustainability of the recent profit growth. While we note CSX achieved similar EBIT margins to last year, revenue grew by a solid 15% to US$15b. That's a real positive.In the chart below, you can see how the company has grown earnings and revenue, over time. For finer detail, click on the image.earnings-and-revenue-historyIn investing, as in life, the future matters more than the past. So why not check out this free interactive visualization of CSX's forecast profits?Are CSX Insiders Aligned With All Shareholders?We would not expect to see insiders owning a large percentage of a US$69b company like CSX. But we are reassured by the fact they have invested in the company. We note that their impressive stake in the company is worth US$189m. This comes in at 0.3% of shares in the company, which is a fair amount of a business of this size. This should still be a great incentive for management to maximise shareholder value.Story continuesIt's good to see that insiders are invested in the company, but are remuneration levels reasonable? Well, based on the CEO pay, you'd argue that they are indeed. Our analysis has discovered that the median total compensation for the CEOs of companies like CSX, with market caps over US$8.0b, is about US$12m.CSX's CEO took home a total compensation package worth US$9.4m in the year leading up to December 2022. That comes in below the average for similar sized companies and seems pretty reasonable. CEO remuneration levels are not the most important metric for investors, but when the pay is modest, that does support enhanced alignment between the CEO and the ordinary shareholders. Generally, arguments can be made that reasonable pay levels attest to good decision-making.Is CSX Worth Keeping An Eye On?One positive for CSX is that it is growing EPS. That's nice to see. The growth of EPS may be the eye-catching headline for CSX, but there's more to bring joy for shareholders. With company insiders aligning themselves considerably with the company's success and modest CEO compensation, there's no arguments that this is a stock worth looking into. We don't want to rain on the parade too much, but we did also find 1 warning sign for CSX that you need to be mindful of.There's always the possibility of doing well buying stocks that are not growing earnings and do not have insiders buying shares. column4: Buy Vail Resorts & CSX, steer clear of CVS & FirstEnergy: Portfolio manager
column10: [Buy Vail Resorts to take advantage of consumer spending, but maybe wait hold off on CVS because of regulatory pressure on drug prices. Zacks Investment Management Client Portfolio Manager Brian Mulberry shares some of his top stock trades with Yahoo Finance Live.Video TranscriptAKIKO FUJITA: Well, the CPI data may have the markets moving today. But it's time to take a longer term look at the potential hotspots for investing in the second half of 2023. To give us his take on what stocks we should be buying right now and the ones to avoid, let's bring in Brian Mulberry, Client Portfolio Manager at Zacks Investment Management.We're going to start with your picks, what you like right now. Vail Resort, specifically, you're looking at the travel space right now. That stock not at the highs-- you know, still below the high of the year. But we have seen consumers, despite some headwinds and concerns about higher prices, shelling out on travel.BRIAN MULBERRY: Yeah, absolutely. It's a way to access the consumer in a slightly different way, where we're seeing the revenge travel trade is still occurring. What we're noticing about Vail in particular is that season pass sales are up about 6%. And they're having a really good recapture rate when it comes to renewing pass holders from last year. And on top of that, they've actually been able to increase prices. So actual sales in dollars are up 11% on that 6% higher season pass sale.So we're looking at a way to take advantage of the consumer spending that has been really durable over the last year. And it's one of the reasons we like Vail. Vail has also done a great job of providing a different menu of passes available and also different destinations. Now, international, we're seeing very strong demand for their resorts in Australia. And there's been some great cross-selling opportunities for consumers internationally to access the US mountains and markets, and then obviously, for US consumers to travel abroad.Story continuesAnd so we're definitely still seeing consumers spend money at a very high rate. And it's one of those ways that we can access this type of a stock at a good price that's still set to continue to grow.SEANA SMITH: But Brian, how should investors be looking at a name like this given the fact that we are still at a risk of recession. There is some signs that the consumer is cracking just a little bit, pulling back on some of their spending. Is a name like Vail, is that going to be able to withstand some of that volatility?BRIAN MULBERRY: We think it is, because there's definitely a big dividing line in the consumer right now. And it's simply this, if you owned your home during the pandemic, you had a once-in-a-generation opportunity to refinance your biggest debt, which is usually your mortgage, on your biggest asset, your home, that appreciated probably 30% to 40% in value. You're able to pay off your cars, your student loans, all these other debts and credit cards. And you now have a much cleaner personal balance sheet.Your personal net income is probably in much better shape than it ever was before. And that lends a little bit more consistency to this consumer spending picture that we're seeing. Unfortunately, if you didn't own your home, those are definitely the consumers that are feeling the pinch of high inflation as well as high interest rates at this point in time.And so we're definitely keeping a close eye on it. We're aware of it. But there is a way to still bet on the consumer. And we think this is one of the ways to do that.AKIKO FUJITA: Another stock you're really hot on, CSX. This is in the rail space. What do you like there?BRIAN MULBERRY: What we're seeing is just a really consistent level of volume, in terms of the rail traffic that they have. They've actually been able to grow by almost 40% in terms of their coal transportation. A lot of that coal is going to produce electricity in other places. And so they've been able to keep up with a really high level of demand. And the execution in the transportation space is one of those things that leads to better margins overall.So again, not a huge valuation. It's one of those ways to invest in something that doesn't have a gigantic PE forward multiple but also has really good, durable earnings. They're also rewarding shareholders by raising their dividend. They actually increase their dividend by 10% earlier this year. And so it's a way to be a little bit more defensive in your allocation.But we also believe that energy overall might be a better place in the second half of the year. And this is just a different way to access those types of returns. Looking at what we've seen in terms of the price of coal and now demand for it coming up, it's going to be a better back half of the year for these types of names in our opinion.SEANA SMITH: Brian, one of the names that you're advising investors to stay away from is CVS. We know the stock has been under pressure now for some time, off pretty significantly since the start of the year. What do you see as pressuring the company here going forward?BRIAN MULBERRY: Well, there's a couple of different reasons that we see, I think, a material decline in both profitability and overall earnings. And obviously, it's one being that they're not getting reimbursed for COVID testing and COVID vaccines at nearly the rate that they were a year or two years ago.But also, in addition to that, you know, there's a lot of regulatory pressure on prices at pharmacies for drugs. And that's good for consumers, but it's net bad for the balance sheet for somebody like CVS when we're seeing more generic drugs available but less reimbursement coming from distributing those generic drugs. It's kind of a double whammy on a company like CVS, where they're not getting the reimbursement from COVID protocols. And now, there's pressure on prices at the pharmacy, which is normally, you know, their top breadwinner, if you will, in terms of generating that revenue.So we think it's going to be a bit of a tough slog for CVS for the next couple of quarters until they can kind of get things figured out where their margins might be headed.AKIKO FUJITA: And finally, Brian, you were talking about some opportunities in the energy spaces. Next name-- next name not necessarily one that you would encourage investors to stay on top of. What are the concerns you have with FirstEnergy?BRIAN MULBERRY: FirstEnergy kind of has an aging grid, if you will. This is a power utility. And while there is a lot of demand for electricity, the way that it's been generated has not been profitable for them. And unfortunately, it's a publicly traded utility that has price caps, if you will. They have to get permission in order to raise their rates to be more profitable in most of the markets that they serve.They've been having a difficult time accessing equipment, maintaining equipment. And like I said, their aging grid is really just been a drag on their overall profitability. So this is one of those energy type names that we would avoid, because it just seems like their execution is a little bit behind the curve. And this is one of those things where certainly the supply chain has affected their ability to get the parts that they need to upgrade their grid and their distribution facilities for sure.But it's definitely weighing on their overall earnings and profitability picture. So this is a name that we would be cautious of in the next couple of quarters.SEANA SMITH: All right. Brian Mulberry of Zacks Investment Management, thanks.]

column4: AAR sues Ohio over 2-person train crew law
column10: [CSX operates in Ohio, where there is a new state law governing train crew sizes. (Photo: Jim Allen/FreightWaves)The Association of American Railroads (AAR) has filed a lawsuit against the state of Ohio, saying federal law preempts a new state law that dictates a minimum crew size for freight rail operations.Ohio’s law, signed by Gov. Mike DeWine on March 31, requires at least two individuals to be involved in moving a freight train in Ohio. The state may issue civil penalties for violations.A number of federal laws preempt Ohio’s law, argued AAR in a petition filed June 29 with the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio. These include the Regional Rail Reorganization Act of 1973 or 3R Act, which came out of freight rail service disruptions in the Northeast and Midwest; the ICC Termination Act, which grants the Surface Transportation Board authority to regulate certain matters; and the Federal Railroad Safety Act.The only Class I railroads that operate in the state are Canadian railway CN (NYSE: CNI), CSX (NASDAQ: CSX) and Norfolk Southern (NYSE: NSC). CSX and NS currently use single-person crews for certain yard operations, including remote control switching operations, AAR said.Ohio law is also more restrictive than a proposed regulation currently before the Federal Railroad Administration on train crew size because FRA’s rule would exempt particular types of trains or trains under specified conditions and has a special approval process for existing one-person crew operations, according to AAR. But Ohio’s law applies to every train or light engine used in connection with the movement of freight, with limited exceptions, AAR said.AAR also cited two studies from consulting firms Oliver Wyman and ICF International, which determined that available safety data and accident rates show no adverse safety impacts resulting from one-person crews versus two-person crews.AAR’s members will “suffer harm to their rights to collectively bargain over crew size. The carriers that operate in Ohio have the right to bargain for system-wide changes in crew size. The Crew Size Law will interfere with the railroads’ ability to expand their rights to operate with one-person crews in Ohio through collective bargaining,” attorneys for AAR said in the court filing.Story continuesCalifornia, Wisconsin, West Virginia, Arizona, Kansas, Minnesota, Washington, Nevada and Colorado also have state laws requiring freight train crews to have at least two people on board, according to the International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail, and Transportation Workers – Transportation Division (SMART-TD).States that have or have had legislation that calls for two-person crews include Illinois, New York and Pennsylvania, SMART-TD said.Subscribe to FreightWaves’ e-newsletters and get the latest insights on freight right in your inboxClick here for more FreightWaves articles by Joanna Marsh.Related links:Sick leave, crew consists still on the table between unions, railroadsTrain length and train crew sizes see state legislative actionUnion Pacific, SMART-TD agree to suspend train crew reconfigurationNS, SMART-TD to hold off on conductor redeployment talksTrain crew size bill advances in New Mexico LegislatureThe post AAR sues Ohio over 2-person train crew law appeared first on FreightWaves.]

column4: Do CSX's (NASDAQ:CSX) Earnings Warrant Your Attention?
column10: [The excitement of investing in a company that can reverse its fortunes is a big draw for some speculators, so even companies that have no revenue, no profit, and a record of falling short, can manage to find investors. Unfortunately, these high risk investments often have little probability of ever paying off, and many investors pay a price to learn their lesson. While a well funded company may sustain losses for years, it will need to generate a profit eventually, or else investors will move on and the company will wither away.In contrast to all that, many investors prefer to focus on companies like CSX (NASDAQ:CSX), which has not only revenues, but also profits. Even if this company is fairly valued by the market, investors would agree that generating consistent profits will continue to provide CSX with the means to add long-term value to shareholders. See our latest analysis for CSX How Quickly Is CSX Increasing Earnings Per Share?If you believe that markets are even vaguely efficient, then over the long term you'd expect a company's share price to follow its earnings per share (EPS) outcomes. Therefore, there are plenty of investors who like to buy shares in companies that are growing EPS. CSX managed to grow EPS by 15% per year, over three years. That growth rate is fairly good, assuming the company can keep it up.Careful consideration of revenue growth and earnings before interest and taxation (EBIT) margins can help inform a view on the sustainability of the recent profit growth. While we note CSX achieved similar EBIT margins to last year, revenue grew by a solid 15% to US$15b. That's a real positive.In the chart below, you can see how the company has grown earnings and revenue, over time. For finer detail, click on the image.earnings-and-revenue-historyIn investing, as in life, the future matters more than the past. So why not check out this free interactive visualization of CSX's forecast profits?Are CSX Insiders Aligned With All Shareholders?We would not expect to see insiders owning a large percentage of a US$69b company like CSX. But we are reassured by the fact they have invested in the company. We note that their impressive stake in the company is worth US$189m. This comes in at 0.3% of shares in the company, which is a fair amount of a business of this size. This should still be a great incentive for management to maximise shareholder value.Story continuesIt's good to see that insiders are invested in the company, but are remuneration levels reasonable? Well, based on the CEO pay, you'd argue that they are indeed. Our analysis has discovered that the median total compensation for the CEOs of companies like CSX, with market caps over US$8.0b, is about US$12m.CSX's CEO took home a total compensation package worth US$9.4m in the year leading up to December 2022. That comes in below the average for similar sized companies and seems pretty reasonable. CEO remuneration levels are not the most important metric for investors, but when the pay is modest, that does support enhanced alignment between the CEO and the ordinary shareholders. Generally, arguments can be made that reasonable pay levels attest to good decision-making.Is CSX Worth Keeping An Eye On?One positive for CSX is that it is growing EPS. That's nice to see. The growth of EPS may be the eye-catching headline for CSX, but there's more to bring joy for shareholders. With company insiders aligning themselves considerably with the company's success and modest CEO compensation, there's no arguments that this is a stock worth looking into. We don't want to rain on the parade too much, but we did also find 1 warning sign for CSX that you need to be mindful of.There's always the possibility of doing well buying stocks that are not growing earnings and do not have insiders buying shares.
